content: A nasal voice refers to a specific type of speaking voice that is characterized by a distinct nasal quality. This quality can occur naturally due to genetic variations. In the context of vocal characteristics, the opposite of a nasal voice is described as adenoidal or denasal. Nasal speech can be further categorized into two types: hypo-nasal and hyper-nasal speech. Hypo-nasal speech occurs when there is an insufficient amount of nasal airflow during speech. This results in a voice that sounds as though the individual has a severe cold. The causes of hypo-nasal speech are typically related to conditions that obstruct the nasal passages. These include, but are not limited to, the following: Enlargement of the adenoids (adenoid hypertrophy) Swelling or enlargement of the nasal turbinates (turbinate hypertrophy) Allergic reactions affecting the nasal passages Sinus infections Viral upper respiratory infections A deviated nasal septum Hyper-nasal speech, on the other hand, is characterized by an excessive amount of nasal airflow during speech. This is particularly noticeable with plosive and fricative sounds, which are syllables that begin with consonants. Examples of conditions that can lead to hyper-nasal speech include cleft palate and velopharyngeal insufficiency, both of which impair the proper closure of the velopharyngeal mechanism, allowing excessive air to escape through the nose during speech.
